extracted.intended_audience: artists, critics, and educated readers interested in aesthetics and art criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for recognizing true art versus counterfeit art across literary, musical, and visual arts — as argued in a philosophical/critical essay. Focuses on how art infects, internal standards, and structural causes of false art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art as contagion / transmission of feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: A real artist, by his work, transmits to others the feeling he experienced; if transmitted, people feel it — that is the essence of art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a work is good as art, the feeling expressed by the artist transmits itself to other people; if it infects, interpretation is superfluous. Example: true works (e.g., Pushkin’s short poems) infect and are felt by readers. Anti-pattern: works that fail to ‘infect’ cannot be rescued by explanations or criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art cannot be fully explained in words
rubrics_metrics.description: If the artist could have conveyed his feeling in words he would have done so; the fact he used art indicates his feeling could not be otherwise transmitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The interpretation of works of art by words indicates the interpreter is incapable of feeling the infection of art. Critics who try to 'explain' art reveal their incapacity for the direct experience art demands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal criterion: religious perception for universal art
rubrics_metrics.description: Universal (folk) art has an indubitable internal criterion — religious perception or a common understanding-of-life shared by the whole people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When art is appraised by the religious/common perception of the people it has an internal standard. By contrast, art of the upper classes lacks this internal standard and thus relies on external authorities, which is misleading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Danger of external criteria / authority-based valuation
rubrics_metrics.description: Upper-class art lacks an internal criterion and so appreciators cling to external criteria — judgments of the 'finest-nurtured' or tradition — which mislead and perpetuate mistaken valuations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics repeat traditions and treat earlier authority-approved works (Dante, Shakespeare, Raphael, Bach, Beethoven) as uniformly admirable, encouraging imitation of 'great' masters even when those standards no longer fit. Result: perversion of taste and proliferation of counterfeit works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wholeness and indivisibility (entirety) of true art
rubrics_metrics.description: A true work of art has such entirety and completeness that the smallest alteration (a line, scene, bar) would disturb the meaning of the whole work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In genuine poems, dramas, pictures, songs, or symphonies one cannot extract or reorder parts without infringing the life of the whole. Counterfeit works lack this property and permit transpositions without altering their apparent 'sense' (example: critique of Wagner’s later music).

rubrics_metrics.name: Infinitely small 'wee bit' degrees determine artistic perfection
rubrics_metrics.description: Art depends on finding infinitely minute degrees — a 'wee bit' lighter, darker, later, earlier — which give the work its infectious quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These minute gradations are what make a rendition infectious; they cannot be taught by external technique but must be found by yielding to feeling. Examples across arts: exact center of a musical pitch; precise timing in dramatic intonation; right shade in painting; perfect word choice in poetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific musical execution criteria (pitch, time, strength)
rubrics_metrics.description: Musical execution is art only when the pitch is exactly right, the note lasts exactly as needed, and the strength (dynamics) is neither more nor less than required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Slight deviations in pitch, timing, or strength destroy perfection and the infectiousness of music. Musical feeling requires the performer to find infinitely small degrees that cannot be instilled by technical instruction alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Creative freedom from preconceived demands
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the chief conditions of artistic creation is the artist’s complete freedom from every kind of preconceived demand; precomposition or adjustment to external requirements destroys creative power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Necessity of adjusting a musical work to a text (or any art to another) is a preconceived demand that prevents genuine creation. Example: Wagner’s requirement that music serve poetry undermines musical creativity; when an artist prescribes the audience’s emotion in advance, it breeds distrust and resistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Each art has its own definite realm — unions generally destroy both
rubrics_metrics.description: Each art has a specific realm and aims; combining two arts in one production (e.g., dramatic poetry + music as Wagner proposes) makes it impossible to fulfill the demands of both fully.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While lyrical poetry and music can sometimes coincide because they share the aim of producing a mental condition, epic or dramatic poetry cannot be made to coincide fully with music. If two arts entirely coincide, they are likely both counterfeits or one is counterfeit. Examples: hymns/songs (partial coincidence), Wagner’s attempts (criticized as artificial and destructive).

rubrics_metrics.name: Art schools cannot teach true art (they teach imitation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Schools can teach techniques and how to transmit feelings experienced by other artists, but they cannot evoke feeling or teach how to manifest one’s own unique feeling — therefore they cannot teach true art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Professional schools produce imitations and methods of former masters (drawing from copies, declaiming monologues like celebrated tragedians, formulaic musical theory), which lead to counterfeit art and desensitize audiences to true art. Suggested alternative: elementary instruction to enable talented pupils to perfect themselves later independently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professionalisation of artists fosters counterfeit art
rubrics_metrics.description: When art becomes a profession (artists living by remuneration from editors, impresarios, publishers), professionalism becomes a primary condition for diffusion of false, counterfeit art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Professional incentives lead artists to produce works to order or in styles that sell, rather than to express unique felt experience. This professionalisation interacts with criticism and schools to flood the market with counterfeits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artistic criticism as a source of perversion
rubrics_metrics.description: Art criticism — valuation by erudite, self-confident individuals rather than by the plain people’s feeling — perverts taste by valorizing brain-spun, invented works and setting misleading authoritative standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics, often less susceptible to art’s contagion, praise works not because they infect but because they conform to theories or tradition (e.g., praise of Greek tragedians, Dante, Beethoven's late period). They thus promote imitation of 'models' and legitimize counterfeits; criticism grows only on upper-class art that lacks an internal criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Techniques/methods of counterfeiting art: borrowings, imitation, effects, interestingness
rubrics_metrics.description: Counterfeit art is produced by combining borrowings, imitation, theatrical/technical effects, and 'interestingness' rather than genuine infection or sincere expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wagner’s works are presented as a model example where subject-matter borrowed from antiquity, imitative decorations/costumes/sounds, striking stage effects (monsters, fires, invisible orchestra) and manufactured 'interest' (complex relations of leit-motifs to objects/characters) are all used to create a convincing but counterfeit art. These are signs to watch for when judging authenticity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predetermination and prescribed emotion are anti-artistic
rubrics_metrics.description: An author’s evident predetermination to elicit specific emotions (e.g., telling the reader to prepare to cry) destroys the authentic emotional response and is characteristic of false art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Predetermined emotional cues produce distrust and prevent genuine infection. Example: theatrical stunts, contrived stage effects, or obvious manipulative writing that signals to the audience what they should feel rather than allowing spontaneous contagion.
